after.abstract: Background: Takotsubo syndrome, which predominantly affects women, is thought to be precipitated by catecholamine excess, yet unstable patients often receive intravenous inotropes. We examined the association between intravenous inotropes and 30-day mortality in a nationwide cohort. Methods: We identified all patients with a first angiographic diagnosis of Takotsubo syndrome in the Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry from 2008 through August 2025, linked to coronary care and population registers. The primary analysis was a Cox model for 30-day death among patients with a coronary care record, adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and Killip class, with multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses varied the covariates and standard errors and examined days 0 to 7 and 8 to 30 separately, and the association was estimated in women and men with an interaction term. Results: Of 3,458 patients (79.4% women), 141 (4.1%) received inotropes: 3.6% of women and 5.8% of men. Thirty-day mortality was 19.9% in treated and 1.7% in untreated patients. The unadjusted hazard ratio was 12.89 (95% CI, 8.20 to 20.26) and the adjusted hazard ratio 6.49 (3.49 to 12.08; P<0.001; E-value, 12.5). In sensitivity analyses, the hazard ratio ranged from 3.37 (1.88 to 6.03), with presenting symptom and laboratory values added, to 6.62 (3.63 to 12.08). The hazard ratio was 8.82 (4.47 to 17.39) for days 0 to 7 and 2.47 (0.65 to 9.36) for days 8 to 30, and 6.43 (3.15 to 13.16) in women and 6.59 (2.79 to 15.58) in men (P=0.96 for interaction). Conclusions: Intravenous inotropes were associated with higher 30-day mortality in Takotsubo syndrome, in both women and men, with most of the excess in the first week.

after.title: Preprint: A model-based approach to identifying atypical type 2 diabetes: UK population-based study
after.authors: Dinsdale, M. M.; McGovern, A. P.; Cardoso, P.; Güdemann, L. M.; Jansz, T. T.; Jones, A. G.; Hattersley, A. T.; McKinley, T. J.; Shields, B. M.; Young, K. G.; Dennis, J. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Clinical and Biomedical Sciences, University of Exeter Medical School, Exeter, UK
after.abstract: Aims Approaches to meaningfully identify individuals with differing prognosis at type 2 diabetes diagnosis are lacking. We aimed to assess whether QDiabetes, a validated routine clinical feature-based model to predict risk of type 2 diabetes onset, could be applied at the point of diagnosis to identify people with atypical type 2 diabetes with differing risk of complications and treatment requirements. Methods We included adults newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2013-2023 in population-representative UK primary care data (Clinical Practice Research Datalink). Individuals with low predicted QDiabetes risk ([≤]5.6%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes and matched up to 1:4 by age, sex and calendar year to typical type 2 diabetes (QDiabetes risk >5.6%). We compared 10-year risks of microvascular, macrovascular, acute complications, mortality and glucose-lowering treatment initiation. For complications, multivariable Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs), adjusting for age, sex, year of diagnosis, ethnicity, deprivation and baseline HbA1c. Results Of 276,117 individuals newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, 30,397 (11.0%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes using our approach. Compared with the wider typical type 2 diabetes population (n=245,720; 89.0%), they were younger (54 vs 60 years), leaner (26.4 vs 34.0 kg/m2) and had higher HbA1c at diagnosis (68.0 vs 60.0 mmol/mol). In matched analyses, the atypical type 2 diabetes group had a higher risk of severe retinopathy (aHR 1.33, 95% CI 1.23-1.44), similar risk of severe neuropathy (aHR 0.92, 0.84-1.01), and lower risk of severe nephropathy (aHR 0.81, 0.73-0.90). Despite lower predicted baseline cardiovascular risk in those with atypical type 2 diabetes, risks of myocardial infarction (aHR 0.99, 0.89-1.11) and stroke (aHR 0.92, 0.81-1.04) were similar, while heart failure risk was lower (aHR 0.72, 0.67-0.78). Atypical type 2 diabetes was also associated with higher risks of diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycaemia, non-cardiovascular mortality and insulin initiation. Conclusion Type 2 diabetes onset risk prediction models used at the point of diagnosis may represent a pragmatic approach to identify people with an atypical type 2 diabetes phenotype. Despite fewer conventional risk factors, the phenotype identified had a poor prognosis and could provide a practical target for personalised type 2 diabetes management to reduce risk of long-term complications.

after.authors: Kebeba, M.; Taa, L.; Alemu, G.; Lema, K.; Kayamo, L.; Oljira, C.; Awol, K.
after.abstract: Background Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in adults with type 2 diabetes(T2DM) and cardiorenal disease, but treatment initiation among eligible patients remains incompletely characterized. We estimated the cumulative incidence of recorded SGLT2 inhibitor initiation and associated participant characteristics in a diverse U.S. cohort. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study leveraging electronic health record data from the All of Us Research Program. Adults with confirmed type 2 diabetes, at least one co-occurring cardiorenal condition (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease), and no prior SGLT2 inhibitor use were followed from the earliest date all criteria were met during 2019-2023. The 365-day cumulative incidence of initiation was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method, accounting for competing risk of all-cause mortality. Cause-specific modified Poisson regression with robust error variance yielded adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) for initiation predictors Results Among 9,333 eligible participants, 637 had recorded SGLT2 inhibitor initiation within 365 days (estimated cumulative incidence, 6.85% (95% CI 6.34-7.36)). The 365-day incidence was 8.40% among individuals with heart failure, 6.65% with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and 5.28% with chronic kidney disease. Initiation was more likely with heart failure (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.29-1.76), and glycated hemoglobin [≥]9.0% versus <7.0% (RR 2.61, 95% CI 2.07-3.28), but less likely with chronic kidney disease (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.54-0.74), age [≥]75 versus 45-64 years (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.40-0.65), and non-Hispanic Black versus non-Hispanic White race and ethnicity (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.97). Conclusions Fewer than 1 in 10 eligible, untreated adults with T2D and cardiorenal disease initiated SGLT2 inhibitor therapy within one year. Even with expanding guideline indications, substantial implementation gaps persist, particularly among patients with CKD, older adults, and non-Hispanic Black adults. Targeted health systems are imperative to optimize the use of guideline-recommended cardiorenal therapies.

after.authors: Mwale, M.; Siame, L.; Mombotwa, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Center for Infectious Diseases Research in Zambia
after.abstract: Abstract Background. Transfer-out is a common outcome in HIV treatment programmes, and transfers that are not documented ("silent transfers") are often misclassified as loss to follow up. Understanding why recipients of care move between facilities, and which reasons lead to undocumented moves, can guide retention strategies. We estimated the incidence of transfer-out and described patient-reported reasons for formal and silent transfer among people receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) in Ndola District, Zambia. Methods. We conducted a cross-sectional study in 11 ART facilities between April and October 2026. All recipients of care who transferred during the study period and consented were interviewed using a World Health Organization (WHO)-adapted questionnaire: formal transfers at exit and silent transfers by telephone once re-engagement elsewhere was established. Reasons were coded into structural, psychosocial and clinic-based domains. We report proportions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and used Firth penalized logistic regression to identify factors associated with silent rather than formal transfer. Results. Of 9,866 recipients of care on ART, 120 transferred out (cumulative incidence 1.22%; 95% CI 1.02-1.45%). The median age was 41 years (IQR 32-48.5) and 61.3% were female; 12 (10.0%) were silent transfers. Structural reasons accounted for 90.8% (95% CI 84.3-94.8) of transfers: work, education or business (55.0%), relocation (32.5%) and distance or transport (3.3%). Psychosocial reasons (marriage or family obligations) accounted for 9.2% (95% CI 5.2-15.7), and no participant reported a clinic-based reason. Silent transfer was more frequent among those reporting psychosocial than structural reasons (45.5% vs 6.4%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 11.36 (2.75-49.56)). Silent transfers were younger than formal transfers (median 33 vs 41 years; P = 0.031), while sex was not associated with transfer type. Conclusions. Transfer-out in Ndola District was uncommon and driven almost entirely by mobility linked to work and relocation rather than dissatisfaction with care. Transfers prompted by marriage or family obligations were much more likely to be undocumented. Asking recipients of care about upcoming life changes, offering facilitated transfers, and using a shared electronic health record could keep mobile recipients of care visible in the HIV programme.

after.title: Preprint: Personal HbA1c trajectories and incident diabetes: association, prediction and observability in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing
after.authors: Tapias, D.; Donati, C.; Völter-Mahlknecht, S.
after.abstract: Background. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individual's typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each person's usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the person's usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. Results. The analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02--1.36, and 1.39, 1.11--1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the person's usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81--1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77--81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. Conclusions. Estimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.

after.title: Preprint: Missing Outcomes and Treatment Effect Estimates in the A4 Study of Solanezumab
after.authors: Jang, E. Y.; Sims, K. D.; Flanders, M.; Ackley, S. F.
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Missing final-visit outcome measurements may bias treatment effect estimates in amyloid-targeting drug trials. We examined whether accounting for missing Week-240 outcomes changed estimated treatment differences in the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial. METHODS: We reanalyzed 1,169 randomized participants, assessing baseline-to-Week-240 change in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) Centiloids, the Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC), and Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) score. We compared available-case estimates with inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW; primary analysis) and multiple imputation under missing at random (MAR), and assessed departures from MAR with delta-adjusted missing not at random (MNAR) analyses. RESULTS: Week-240 amyloid PET, PACC, and CDR-SB were missing for 352 (30.1%), 345 (29.5%), and 343 (29.3%) participants. IPCW treatment differences (solanezumab minus placebo) were -8.74 Centiloids (95% bootstrap CI, -11.75 to -5.86), -0.076 PACC points (CI, -0.691 to 0.517), and 0.126 CDR-SB points (CI, -0.077 to 0.320). These were close to the available-case differences of -8.56 Centiloids, -0.100 PACC points, and 0.120 CDR-SB points, and the MAR imputation differences. Assuming missing solanezumab outcomes were 0.50 SD worse than MAR predictions, differences were -3.48 Centiloids (95% CI, -6.50 to -0.46), -0.981 PACC points (CI, -1.602 to -0.360), and 0.297 CDR-SB points (CI, 0.112 to 0.481). DISCUSSION: Methods assuming that missingness is explained by measured data did not change the A4 findings. The amyloid result withstood large departures from this assumption, but PACC and CDR-SB results became unfavorable under modest ones, so conclusions for these outcomes depend on why data are missing.

after.title: Preprint: AI Identification of Transdiagnostic Factors in Adolescent Mental Health
after.authors: Luo, L.; Cummins, N.; Michelini, G.; Wise, T.; Iniesta, R.
after.abstract: Background: Adolescent psychopathology is commonly assessed using high-dimensional questionnaire data. These data often consist of ordinal, sparse, and overlapping symptom items, creating challenges for deriving latent phenotypes that are both interpretable and generalisable. This study addressed the need to derive low-dimensional transdiagnostic phenotypes from adolescent mental health data by evaluating denoising autoencoders as a flexible non-linear representation-learning approach. Methods: Using baseline data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, we analysed mental health questionnaire data from a large community sample of adolescents (N = 9,799). A denoising autoencoder was trained to learn low-dimensional latent representations and was benchmarked against principal component analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and radial basis function kernel principal component analysis using held-out reconstruction explained variance. Interpretability was assessed using item-level canonical correlation analyses and alignment with a framework of well-established psychopathology dimensions. External validity was examined using gradient-boosted tree models predicting clinical and functional validators. Results: Across three to five factors solutions, the autoencoder consistently achieved the highest reconstruction explained variance compared with all benchmark methods. The five-factor autoencoder solution showed interpretable correspondence with established dimensional structures of psychopathology, rather than mapping onto a single general factor. Autoencoder-derived factors showed equal or modestly superior predictive validity compared with EFA across most validator domains. Conclusions: These findings suggest that denoising autoencoders may offer a useful complementary approach for deriving low-dimensional, interpretable, and externally valid transdiagnostic phenotypes from adolescent symptom data, with potential utility for summarising complex symptom profiles and supporting dimensional assessment in clinical and research settings.

after.title: Preprint: Classifying chronic kidney disease from non-invasive questionnaire features in adults with long-standing diabetes in Bangladesh: model development, internal validation and the limits of small-sample evidence
after.authors: Anan, A.; Arshi, U. T.; Islam, R. N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology
after.abstract: Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common complication of diabetes, and in Bangladesh laboratory testing for it is not always available. Questionnaire answers could help decide whom to test first, but small machine-learning studies often report optimistic accuracy. Methods We analysed a public dataset of 400 adults with at least 10 years of diabetes attending a tertiary hospital in Dhaka, 185 with a hospital diagnosis of CKD. A pre-specified ridge logistic regression using 20 non-invasive features was developed and internally validated with nested cross-validation (five folds, ten repeats), compared with lasso, random forest and gradient boosting, and assessed for discrimination, calibration and net benefit. Simulations examined case-enriched sampling and single train/test splits. Results The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval 0.70-0.80; optimism-corrected 0.76). Flexible algorithms were not detectably better (differences -0.005 to +0.006). Calibration within the sample was good (slope 1.06, 0.79-1.33), and testing the highest-scoring 30% of patients would have found 48% of CKD cases. The sample was smaller than the 883 patients recommended. Urinary infection, body-mass index, insulin use, diabetes duration and pain-killer use were positively associated with CKD and diet adherence negatively; regular walking and hypertension showed directions opposite to clinical expectation, consistent with features recorded after diagnosis. The yearly history added no reliable information. In simulation, case-enriched sampling preserved the AUC but overstated absolute risk (mean predicted risk 0.37 at a true prevalence of 0.10). Over 300 random 80/20 splits of the same data, the test AUC ranged from 0.61 to 0.87; reporting the best of ten splits would overstate it by about 0.07. Conclusions Questionnaire features moderately distinguished patients with an existing CKD diagnosis. Whether they identify patients before diagnosis requires external validation in patients assessed before CKD status is known. The study was not registered.

after.title: Preprint: Remote auditory task performance, cognition, and APOE4 across two dementia-risk cohorts
after.authors: Happs, C.; Toma, A.; Koychev, I.; Malhotra, P.; O'Brien, J.; Ritchie, C.; Muniz-Terrera, G.; Lad, M.
after.abstract: Background. Difficulty hearing speech in noise is associated with cognitive ageing and dementia risk. It is unclear whether performance on remote auditory tasks reflects the apolipoprotein E (APOE) {epsilon}4 allele, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimers disease, or broader cognitive and ageing processes. Methods. We analysed two independent cohorts: the Great Minds research register of older adults and the mid-life PREVENT Dementia programme. Both completed the same remote auditory battery: digits-in-noise, speech-in-babble, auditory working-memory precision for tone frequency and for amplitude-modulation rate, and the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index. Cognitive outcomes were paired-associate learning in Great Minds, and the Four Mountains Task, Supermarket Task and selected COGNITO scores in PREVENT. Associations were tested with covariate-adjusted robust regression and false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction. Results. The analytic samples comprised 164 Great Minds and 90 PREVENT participants (mean age 70.6 vs 56.8 years). APOE {epsilon}4 carrier status was not associated with any auditory measure in either cohort (all FDR-corrected p>0.70). In Great Minds, better speech-in-babble performance and better amplitude-modulation-rate working-memory precision were each associated with better paired-associate learning (both FDR-corrected p=0.019). In PREVENT, no auditory measure was associated with spatial-memory or COGNITO scores after age and sex adjustment and FDR correction. Conclusions. Remote auditory task performance was associated with memory in the older cohort but not with APOE {epsilon}4 carrier status in either cohort, although the samples could not exclude small genotype effects. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether remote auditory testing predicts cognitive change.

after.title: Preprint: Rethink the Flow: Establishing a Preanalytical Workflow for Protein Detection in Menstrual Effluent.
after.authors: Denuga, S.; Lukaszczyk, B.; Okwuegbuna, T.; Suryoharaharjo, K.; Ogata, A.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Menstrual effluent (ME) is a promising, minimally invasive biofluid that contains unique protein biomarkers indicative of systemic and gynecological health. Despite its potential, the adoption of ME as a biofluid for disease identification remains limited because no standardized protocols exist for sample collection, processing, and storage. The lack of standardization remains a major challenge in ME research, introducing non-biological variability that limits accurate protein measurements and downstream interpretation for disease diagnosis. We examine how preanalytical factors, including centrifugation, freeze-thaw cycling, and pre-processing storage conditions, affect sample stability and protein concentration measurements. METHODS: Single-molecule array (Simoa) technology was used to quantify cancer antigen 125 (CA125) in ME samples collected from 19 participants. RESULTS: We found that delays in sample processing beyond eight hours increased the probability of unsuccessful fractionation (p < 0.02), a metric of sample stability. We detected CA125 in 100% of ME and ME-derived plasma samples; however, plasma showed better reproducibility across aliquots. Repeated freeze-thaw cycling significantly altered CA125 concentrations in plasma samples. ME samples stored at 4 {degrees} C before centrifugation maintained their ability to fractionate and protein integrity for up to 120 h. We also demonstrate that the developed workflow is compatible with longitudinal monitoring of CA125 in ME over three consecutive cycles. CONCLUSIONS: These results support at-home self-collection of ME for sample acquisition. Furthermore, the developed workflow enabled reliable protein biomarker analysis, facilitating the use of ME as a biofluid for biomarker discovery for gynecological diseases

after.authors: Ma, Y.; Dey, A. K.; Aguilera, R.; Letellier, N.; Scala, P.; Gershunov, A.; Walker, A.; Jones-Ngo, C. G.; Jerrett, M.; Connolly, R.; Thakur, N.; Marlier, M. E.; Benmarhnia, T.
after.abstract: Rationale: Wildfire smoke is an increasing public health threat, yet most epidemiologic studies estimate average smoke-health associations across broad spatial or temporal scales. Such approaches may obscure substantial heterogeneity across individual smoke waves, leaving an important evidence gap for dynamic public health preparedness, risk communication, and clinical practice. Objectives: To estimate event-specific excess respiratory acute care utilization during smoke waves and identify smoke wave features associated with higher excess utilization. Methods: We conducted a statewide study of 18,271,754 respiratory acute care encounters in California from 2006 to 2019. A smoke wave was defined as at least 2 consecutive days during which county-level wildfire smoke fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeded the 95th percentile over the study period. We applied a machine learning-integrated two-stage interrupted time-series design to estimate excess respiratory acute care utilization during each event. We then used meta-regressions to examine multiple spatiotemporally varying effect modifiers such as smoke wave duration, intensity, timing, and co-occurring climate and meteorological conditions. Measurements and Main Results: A total of 1,249 smoke waves were identified and examined in this study. Excess respiratory acute care utilization varied substantially across smoke waves. Higher excess utilization was associated with longer smoke wave duration, greater intensity, winter occurrence, short recovery period, overlap with holidays, drought conditions, or co-occurrence with precipitation or extreme heat events. Conclusions: This study proposes a novel analytical framework to systematically evaluate spatiotemporal drivers of heterogeneity in wildfire smoke respiratory health effects. The findings can inform dynamic preparedness and public health response to smoke events.

after.title: Preprint: Non-invasive finger sweat analysis provides distribution-related information for dexamphetamine and zolpidem in humans
after.authors: Wolf, M.; Pfoser-Poschacher, V.; Wasinger, D.; Hahn, G.; Meier-Menches, S.; Wolzt, M.; Gerner, C.
after.abstract: Eccrine sweat reportedly contains information about drug distribution, but its collection is often lengthy and sophisticated. Finger sweat is collected within 3 minutes by standardized extraction of fingertips, simple, and non-invasive. We previously demonstrated that finger sweat indicates drug intake, motivating us to assess its distribution-related information. Thus, two well characterized drugs with contrasting distribution characteristics were chosen for the parallel analysis of finger sweat and plasma samples. Forty participants received a single-dose of 30 mg dexamphetamine hemisulfate or 5 mg zolpidem tartrate (n = 20 per group). Matched finger sweat and plasma samples collected at baseline and 3 and 8 h post-dose were analyzed by mass spectrometry hyphenated with liquid chromatography. Assuming 1 microliter sweat per sample, we calculated apparent finger sweat concentrations and finger sweat-to-total-plasma concentration ratios. All 40 corresponding post-dose samples for each drug were positive and all 80 expected-negative samples were negative. finger sweat-to-total-plasma concentration ratio was approximately 4-fold higher for dexamphetamine compared with zolpidem at 3 h (p = 9.9 10E-6) and 8 h (p = 2.3 10E-5) and approximately doubled from 3 to 8 h for both dexamphetamine (p = 0.013) and zolpidem (p = 6.7 10E-5). The higher finger sweat-to-total-plasma concentration ratio values for dexamphetamine are consistent with its lower plasma protein binding and larger apparent volume of distribution, providing initial evidence that finger sweat may contain distribution-related information. The time-dependent finger sweat-to-total-plasma concentration ratio increases are compatible with slow drug equilibration and retention within the stratum corneum. The present findings warrant further investigation of finger sweat as an easily accessible sample matrix to assess distribution-related drug characteristics.

after.authors: Perez, C.; Alver, S. K.; Pflieger, L.; Quinn-Bohmann, N.; Rappaport, N.; Magis, A. T.; Burk, R. D.; Qi, Q.; Kaplan, R.; Gibbons, S. M.
after.abstract: Antibiotics are among the most widely prescribed drugs, and they reliably disrupt the commensal gut microbiota. Large epidemiological studies link antibiotic exposure to type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk, yet smaller randomized intervention trials have failed to find this connection. Whether this discordance reflects a true lack of signal or subpopulation-dependent responses to antibiotics remains unclear. Here, across three independent cohorts (N=4,122), we show that recent antibiotic use may reshape host physiology in specific dietary, microbial, and metabolic contexts. Recent antibiotic use was associated with reduced gut microbiome richness, greater Bacteroides and pathobiont dominance, lower predicted butyrate production, and altered levels of 34 blood metabolites, including several microbe-host co-metabolites, such as hippurate and isoursodeoxycholic acid, while the blood proteome was unchanged. Diet and microbiome composition influenced the magnitude of these effects: preference for liquor was associated with steeper diversity loss, and the presence of specific bacterial genera either dampened or amplified antibiotic-associated blood metabolite differences. Clinical chemistries did not differ, on average, across antibiotic treament groups, affirming the intervention trials. However, recent antibiotic users with T2D showed elevated methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, and alkaline phosphatase, suggesting B-vitamin deficiency. Furthermore, antibiotic users with poorer metabolic health (e.g., blood metabolomics-inferredBMI > measured BMI) showed lower circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Overall, metabolic disruption associated with recent antibiotic use appears to be related to vitamin deficiencies and is concentrated in metabolically vulnerable subgroups, arguing for further research into context-aware prescribing and targeted co-therapies, like higher fiber diets, probiotics, or supplements.

after.abstract: Objective: Risk stratification for major depressive disorder (MDD) remains limited by clinical heterogeneity and modest genomic prediction. We examined whether integrating family history, polygenic risk scores (PRS), childhood trauma, and background factors improves prediction of lifetime MDD diagnosis and its severity, relative to models including only subsets of these predictors. Methods: Analyses included 9,927 cases and 4,452 controls from the Genetic Links to Anxiety and Depression Study and NIHR BioResource (GLAD+) and 40,667 cases and 70,755 controls from UK Biobank (UKB). Lifetime MDD was defined using DSM-5 based online assessments. Predictors included family history of multiple psychiatric disorders (mFH), multi-trait PRSs (mPRS), childhood trauma, and background factors (sex and ten genetic principal components). Nested elastic net regression and XGBoost were used to predict MDD within and across cohorts. Results: Multivariable models integrating mFH, mPRS, childhood trauma, and background factors demonstrated strong risk classification (AUC=0.83 in GLAD+; 0.74 in UKB). Family history consistently outperformed multi-trait PRS (GLAD+: 0.74 vs. 0.66; UKB: 0.65 vs. 0.60). External validation showed preserved classification (AUC=0.71-0.82), with attenuation reflecting differences in case severity across cohorts. Models explained up to 27% of the variance in the number of depressive episodes. Conclusions: Multivariable integration of familial, environmental, and genetic factors yields robust and transferable prediction of MDD. Family history and childhood trauma consistently outperform current PRS for both case classification and severity prediction, underscoring the continued importance of integrating clinical data into prediction models in the genomic era.

after.authors: Semahegn, A.; Belete, M.; Tiruneh, G. T.; Siraneh, Y.; Mulu, S.; Teferi, M.; Girma, A.; Walelign, Y.; Muluneh, M. D.; Getnet, A.; Asfaw, M.; Kebede, M.; Tefera, L.; Hagos, K. L.; Ayehu, T.; Alemayehu, Y. K.; Emaway, D.; Taddesse, L.; Makonnen, M.; Tamire, A.; Worku, H.; Argaw, M.
after.abstract: Introduction: Lack of access to essential health services has remained a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. The conventional health service delivery models often fail to account for the mobility patterns and socio-cultural values of these communities. These communities are frequently affected by recurrent droughts, conflicts, floods, and disease outbreaks. This study assessed the contribution of a mobile health services (MHS) delivery model designed to improve access to and utilisation of maternal, neonatal, and child health services in pastoralist contexts of Ethiopia. Methods: A multi-method embedded implementation research with a non-randomized controlled quasi-experimental study design was employed in four selected Woredas of Ethiopia. Baseline data from July 2022 to June 2023 and endline data from July 2023 to June 2024 were extracted from DHIS2. The MHS delivery model was co-designed with stakeholders, redefined communitycentred outreach sites, and established a multidisciplinary team, that was implemented monthly. The average distance between the health facility and the centre of the targeted community village was 29.6 kilometres. Data were captured from routine health service records, MHS databases, and program reports, and 143 in-depth interviews among service providers and beneficiaries. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistical methods and difference-indifferences using Stata 18, while qualitative data were coded and analysed using ATLAS.ti. Results: During the twelve months, the MHS reached 79,404 people through 190 sessions held and offered an integrated essential health service in 20 hard-to-reach villages. In the study area, ANC use was 64.0% in Chifra and 75.6% in Dasenech. In addition, penta-3 antigen vaccination improved from 66.0% to 69.7% in Chifra and from 91.2% to 102.1% in Dasenech, respectively. In the difference-indifferences analysis, the MHS significantly enhanced access to ANC follow-up and completion of pentavalent and full vaccination coverage. A Woreda-led approach, community engagement, context-tailored and timely communication, and comprehensive service delivery by a multidisciplinary team enhanced the use and acceptability of the MHS in the pastoral setting. The contribution of MHS to ensuring access and use of MNCH services ranged from 13.0% to 19.1% for continuing family planning and antenatal care, respectively. Conclusions: The study highlights that the MHS delivery model is a suitable platform that has substantially contributed to improving access to and use of maternal, newborn, and child health services in pastoral, agropastoral, and scattered settlements. Being a woreda-led, participatory codesign, community-centred approach, and context-tailored health service delivery approach enhanced the acceptability and effectiveness of the MHS in reaching the underserved community. Integration of MHS with the existing PHC system, with an innovative, sustainable financing mechanism, is recommended to ensure access and use of MNCH in hard-to-reach settings.

after.authors: Terada, M.; Yeh, T.; Natalia, H.; Baker, L. H.; Torres-Martinez, M.; Bolanle, D.; Shah, H.; Jiwani, U.; Zhang, L.; Park, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Background Since the World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed single-dose HPV vaccination in 2022, many countries have adopted this schedule. However, evidence regarding the schedule changes impact on HPV vaccination coverage remains limited. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, we assessed coverage changes following the schedule switch and explored stakeholders perspectives on factors influencing these trends. Methods Using WHO-UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage, we assessed first-dose HPV vaccination (HPV1) coverage among females in 49 countries that switched to a single-dose schedule during 2022-2024. We used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to compare mean HPV1 coverage before and after the switch, stratified by country and program characteristics. We also examined country-level changes in HPV1 and complete HPV vaccination (HPVc) coverage across all 49 countries. We then qualitatively interviewed 33 national and sub-national HPV vaccination stakeholders from 15 countries and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. Results Following the switch, significant increases in mean HPV1 coverage were observed among non-high-income countries (55.0% pre-switch vs. 63.3% post-switch, p=0.019), countries in the WHO African Region (58.9% vs. 71.6%, p=0.038), and programs employing school-based delivery (57.0% vs. 66.0%, p=0.010). Significant increases were also observed in programs targeting females only (56.3% vs. 65.9%, p=0.040), those targeting single-age cohorts (61.3% vs. 72.0%, p=0.013), and Gavi-supported countries (54.9% vs. 73.2%, p=0.010). Stakeholders attributed coverage trends to multiple factors beyond the schedule change, including recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions, concurrent programmatic changes, and broader contextual factors. Conclusion Although coverage trends varied across countries, improvement in HPV1 coverage in resource-limited settings suggested that the switch to a single-dose schedule may have facilitated recovery from COVID-19-related disruptions. Continued monitoring of vaccination coverage, implementation outcomes, and program sustainability is essential to understanding the long-term population-level implication of the single-dose recommendation.

after.abstract: Chronic tinnitus, the persistent perception of phantom sound, affects 14 to 15\% of adults yet lacks a validated neurophysiological biomarker, in part because group-average EEG analyses obscure the individual heterogeneity that defines the condition. In a multi-site case-control study of 544 participants (268 with tinnitus, mean age 45.4 {+/-} 16.1 years, 52\% female) across seven independent international sites, we applied normative modelling to quantify how far each person's resting-state EEG deviates from age- and hearing-adjusted healthy norms. Fusing spectral-power and connectivity deviations, a classifier detected tinnitus with an area under the curve of 0.832 under site-grouped cross-validation of precomputed normative features. The single most discriminative feature, rank-stable across all seven sites, was theta-band right orbitofrontal (pars orbitalis) connectivity, which dominated attribution by roughly an order of magnitude. Theta hyperconnectivity spanned frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks while primary auditory cortex showed negligible involvement, favouring failed top-down gating over bottom-up auditory overactivity. Features identifying tinnitus presence were orthogonal to symptom severity. These findings reframe chronic tinnitus as a frontoparietal attention-network disorder and nominate right orbitofrontal theta hyperconnectivity as a site-robust diagnostic feature. Data were collected within the TIDE project (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06520865).

after.authors: Mdingi, M. M.; Kullin, B.; Jung, H.; Gigi, R. M.; Babalola, C. M.; Medina-Marino, A. M.; Taylor, C. M.; Muzny, C.; Low, N.; Klausner, J. D.; Peters, R. P.
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Repeat Chlamydia trachomatis positivity after treatment may reflect persistent infection, reinfection, or residual nucleic acid. We compared paired ompA genotypes of C. trachomatis in pregnant women in South Africa and assessed macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Methods: We analyzed paired baseline and follow-up specimens from 43 pregnant women with C. trachomatis detected at two study visits. We determined ompA genotypes by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing and compared genotypes between visits. A fragment of the 23S rRNA gene was sequenced to identify selected macrolide resistance-associated mutations. Results: At baseline, ompA typing was successful in 38/43 (88%) specimens and 36/43 (84%) at follow-up, with paired genotype results available for 32 women (74%). Genotypes E, J and D predominated at baseline and follow-up. The same genotype was detected at both visits in 22/32 women (69%), whereas 10/32 (31%) had a different genotype at follow-up. Genotype concordance was observed in 2/2 (100%) women with paired results at the test-of-cure visit, 13/16 (81%) assessed at 32 weeks gestation, and 7/14 (50%) assessed postnatally. No targeted macrolide resistance associated mutations were detected in specimens with successful 23S rRNA sequencing. Conclusions: One-third of women with paired results had a different ompA genotype at follow-up, consistent with acquisition of a different strain after treatment. Concordant ompA genotypes may reflect persistence or reinfection with a strain sharing the same genotype, acquired from the same or a different partner. Macrolide resistance associated mutations were not detected. High-resolution typing methods would allow more detailed understanding of persistent C. trachomatis test positivity in this population.

after.title: Preprint: Smartphone-Based Assessment of Cognitive Variability in Alzheimer Disease
after.authors: Byun, A. J. S.
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Repeated smartphone testing can measure cognitive inconsistency that a single clinic visit cannot capture. We evaluated cognitive variability and everyday phone use in biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer disease (AD). METHODS: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment due to AD or mild AD dementia and cognitively unimpaired controls used Smartphone Monitoring Assessment in Real Time-Alzheimer (SMART-A) on their own phones. Response-time variability was adjusted for task demand and practice. RESULTS: Among 26 participants with cognitive data (14 controls, 12 AD), the four-marker variability composite was higher in AD (Hedges g = 1.29; 95% confidence interval, 0.53-2.06; P = .003) and correlated with baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment score (r = -0.60; P = .001). Memory-task accuracy was lower in AD at all four trials, and 64.5% versus 98.2% of sessions reached delayed recall (P < .001). Median phone-use bouts were shorter in AD (2.4 vs 5.4 minutes; P = .031), without a detectable pickup-frequency difference. Diary-reported bedtime was earlier in AD; sensor-derived sleep, activity, and mobility showed no statistically detectable differences. None of the 19 cross-domain contrasts survived false-discovery-rate correction. DISCUSSION: SMART-A supported repeated assessment over months in biomarker-confirmed AD. Cognitive variability, memory-task progression, and phone-use duration are promising complementary measures, requiring independent validation of reliability, incremental value, and sensitivity to clinical change.

after.title: Preprint: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
after.authors: Saboo, K. V.; Fan, J. M.; Tadayon, E.; Chang, E. F.; Rao, V. R.; Khambhati, A. N.
after.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

after.abstract: Distinguishing atypical from typical neurodevelopment requires large, well-characterized paediatric cohorts with harmonized multimodal neuroimaging and comprehensive phenotyping. Here, we describe the protocol for the Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (CPIP) Reference Sample, including the design, recruitment strategy, and phenotyping protocol, along with overviews of the imaging and genetics protocols. Using a multisite accelerated longitudinal design, we aim to recruit >800 participants aged 0 to 16 years at baseline, across three Canadian sites (Alberta Childrens Hospital, Calgary; The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Toronto; and CHU Sainte-Justine, Montreal) with comprehensive assessments at baseline and an annual follow-up, with additional follow-ups contingent on project extension. The protocol includes harmonized multimodal neuroimaging, extensive phenotyping across five broad domains: demographic, social and environmental factors; physical health and development; mental health and substance use; cognition; and temperament/personality, as well as DNA sequencing. Exclusion criteria are minimal to ensure a sample representative of the catchment areas of the participating hospitals. Data and protocols will be openly shared with the research community. The C-PIP Reference Sample will provide Canada's first large-scale pediatric neuroimaging reference cohort, enabling researchers to map typical and atypical trajectories from infancy through adolescence, identify biomarkers, examine genetic and contextual influences on brain development, and provide a normative comparison framework for clinical populations.

after.title: Preprint: Beyond billing codes: a proof-of-concept study of large language models for pregnancy episode reconstruction from clinical notes
after.authors: Schalkamp, A.-K.; Azzam, S.; Ayati, A.; Belov, A.; Wang, M.; Rudrapatna, V. A.
after.abstract: Background: Accurate identification of pregnancy episodes from electronic health records (EHRs) is essential for maternal and fetal health research. Existing approaches rely primarily on diagnosis and procedure codes, which may miss pregnancies documented outside the health system and are susceptible to coding errors. Clinical notes contain richer information but remain largely unexplored for this task. Objectives: To evaluate whether a large language model (LLM) can reconstruct complete pregnancy episodes directly from clinical notes. Methods: Chronologically concatenated notes and messages were provided to GPT-5, which identified episodes and extracted variables including assisted reproductive treatment, gestational age, outcome, and complications. Performance was benchmarked against manual chart review (gold standard) and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm in 30 patients comprising 74 pregnancies (20 patients in a held-out test set). Results: The LLM identified 53 of 54 test-set pregnancies versus 40/54 for a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm, with fewer spurious episodes (3 vs 24), corresponding to an F1 score for pregnancy detection against chart review of 0.96 vs 0.68. Among pregnancies identified by both methods, median absolute error was 0 vs 25.5 days for start dates (p<0.001) and 0 vs 1 day for end dates (p=0.044), and outcome accuracy was numerically but not significantly higher (0.84 vs 0.74 for exact outcome types; 0.92 vs 0.84 with abortion subtypes grouped). It additionally recovered information unavailable in structured data, including reproductive-treatment type and fetus-level outcomes. Conclusions: An LLM applied to clinical narratives identified pregnancy episodes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm while capturing richer clinical detail. Because the two approaches used different input data, these gains reflect both the information in clinical notes and the LLM itself. LLM-based extraction from clinical notes is a promising complement to code-based pregnancy phenotyping that warrants evaluation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts.

after.authors: Garcia-Lopez, D.; Hernando, B.; Chaves-Urbano, B.; Escobar-Rey, M.; Gomez-Sanchez, D.; Cadiz, A.; Gallego, A.; Mendiola, M.; Berjon, A.; Caleiras, E.; Garcia, J. F.; Hardisson, D.; Toledo, G.; Redondo, A.; Garcia, M. J.; Macintyre, G.
after.abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.

after.authors: Orcutt, X.; Nimgaonkar, V.; Chen, K.; Riaz, I.; Cohen, A.; Mamtani, R.; Gomes, M.; Long, Q.; Parikh, R. B.
after.abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

items.title: Preprint: CB-COMIL: interpretable prediction of melanoma immunotherapyresponse from multiplex immunofluorescence whole-slide images

after.authors: Rana, P.; Gide, T. N.; Adegoke, N.; Mao, Y.; N. Lo, S.; Berkovsky, S.; Coiera, E.; Long, G. V.; Wilmott, J. S.; Liu, S.
after.abstract: Deep learning models can predict melanoma immunotherapy response but rarely explain predictions biologically. Concept bottleneck models offer interpretable predictions, but have not been applied to multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and whether their learned concepts reproduce tissue measurements remains unclear. We developed CB-COMIL, which routes mIF predictions through four supervised concepts (immune:tumour ratio, CD8/SOX10 balance, CD68 relative signal and PD-L1 evasion index), decomposing each prediction exactly into concept contributions. Developed on 211 slides and evaluated on 42 slides from an independent, differently acquired test cohort, CB-COMIL achieved macro-F1 0.69 versus 0.67 for an opaque comparator (difference 0.020, 95% CI: -0.103 to 0.144). In 41 slides with complete measurements, learned concepts correlated with measured counterparts (Spearman: 0.61; 0.61-0.76), yet substituting measured values reduced macro-F1 from 0.68 to 0.48. CB-COMIL makes predictions interpretable without detectable performance loss, and our evaluation shows that concepts can faithfully determine predictions without reproducing the corresponding biological measurements.

after.title: Preprint: Wearable-measured 24-hour heart rate variability and neovascular age-related macular degeneration: a cross-sectional study
after.authors: Park, D.-W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Casey Eye Institute, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon, USA
after.abstract: Objective To examine wearable heart rate measures in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), reporting an exploratory observation in neovascular AMD. Results This cross-sectional All of Us analysis used minute-level Fitbit heart rate from adults aged [≥]50 years with eye care records. Among the 55 participants with neovascular AMD, the mean date of complete Fitbit recording days fell a median of 1.9 years after the first neovascular AMD diagnosis code. The 7259 comparators had no AMD. The planned primary test, sleeping heart rate with any AMD, was not statistically significant (odds ratio [OR] per 10 beats/min, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.97-1.29). Higher standard deviation of 5-minute average beat intervals (SDANN), a secondary measure, was associated with higher odds of neovascular AMD versus no AMD (OR per 10 ms, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.04-1.21], uncorrected P = 0.002, Bonferroni-adjusted P = 0.051 for 22 comparisons). In an exploratory comparison with non-neovascular AMD, the OR was 1.20 (95% CI, 1.08-1.32). After 24-hour heart rate adjustment, the OR versus no AMD was 1.13 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24). No associations were detected for epiretinal membrane or cataract. This exploratory observation warrants testing in recordings preceding conversion.

after.title: Preprint: A deep multimodal model for age-related macular degeneration detection using optical coherence tomography imaging and clinical text data
after.authors: Fang, M.; Miri, H.; Bishop, K.; Robatjazy, D.; Ko, R. C.; Nrusimhadevara, R.; Cayabyab, F. S.; Ko, S.-B.; Taghibiglou, C.
after.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss, with a significant impact on the elderly population worldwide. Machine learning and deep learning methods, combined with optical coherence tomography (OCT), are promising for the rapid diagnosis of AMD. However, most models focus only on one single OCT imaging modality or neglect clinical information. To improve this problem, we design a deep multimodal framework that integrates OCT images with clinical text data for the detection of AMD. Then, we evaluate the proposed model using metrics, such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F-score, and the area under the curve (AUC), achieving excellent detection results at both the image level and patient level. Next, we conduct computational efficiency analysis and independent external validation to further demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed model.In addition,we provide visualization results with explainable AI technique to further show the effectiveness of the proposed model. Our proposed model using multimodal strategy involving machine learning along with available clinical text and OCT imaging data accurately predicts individuals with AMD. Therefore, the use of machine learning and explainable AI in AMD detection may ultimately improve early diagnosis and offer more precise and personalized treatment strategies, improving the management ofAMD and preservingvision.

after.title: Preprint: Clinical review before execution of executable guideline encodings: a prospective registered study of three ocular hypertension guidelines
after.authors: Ragosta, A.; Bruni, F.
after.abstract: Objective: To determine whether executable encodings of three ocular hypertension guidelines, produced under a prospectively frozen pipeline barring author-defined operationalisations, are judged faithful by independent clinical review before execution, and to characterise findings on retained content, exclusions and divisions. Methods: Under a registered protocol, one ophthalmologist encoded European Glaucoma Society (EGS), American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines; a second encoded a sample. A gate barred author-defined operationalisations. Before execution, two other ophthalmologists reviewed branches, exclusions and division records against predefined materiality criteria. Results: The gate admitted 0, 2 and 1 branches (EGS, AAO, NICE) from 748, 322 and 198 eligible units. Review of these branches raised no primary finding (AAO 0/2, NICE 0/1); at these denominators, uninformative. In the overlap, one NICE omission (laser trabeculoplasty) was judged material. The exclusion reviewer flagged material source-stated decision content in 601/2,109, 216/234 and 151/179 excluded passages. A masked post-hoc reader agreed with 31/50, 11/50 and 28/50 sampled flags; he judged 1/246 passages directly relevant to the initial treat-or-observe decision and 0/100, 0/68 and 8/78 needed to preserve a retained unit's meaning. No synthetic case resolved to observation. Conclusion: Without author-defined choices, few branches were instantiable and none resolved to observation. Fidelity was not determinable at these denominators; exclusion flags were reader-dependent, and some NICE exclusions may have carried meaning needed by retained units. Exclusion review shows what a scope restriction sets aside; its reproducibility must be established before it measures fidelity.

after.authors: Serigatto, H. R.; Kokitsu-Nakata, N. M.; Vendramini-Pittoli, S.; Tonello, C.; Passos-Bueno, M. R.; Zechi-Ceide, R. M.
after.abstract: The oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome is a rare condition characterized by ocular hypertelorism, broad nose, mandibular hypoplasia, preauricular tags, and ear anomalies. Despite presenting a clinically recognizable pattern defined by the overlap of craniofacial microsomia and frontonasal dysplasia, its etiology remains unknown. Males and females are equally affected, and there is no recurrence reported. Genetic investigations performed to date could not clarify this issue yet. To further investigate Mendelian inheritance and test the hypothesis of a possible monogenic cause, we performed exome sequencing in a case series of Brazilian individuals from a single center with the clinical diagnosis of oculoauriculofrontonasal syndrome, including both solo and trio-based exome sequencing. The results provided here further support a non-traditional inheritance model, requiring additional studies including multi-omics approaches to elucidate its etiology.

after.title: Preprint: Optimizing Exomiser to prioritize candidate genes underlying monogenic forms of common disease
after.authors: Petrovska, J.; Rubio-Aliaga, I.; T'Sjoen, D.; Van Wynsberghe, J.; Vanakker, O.; Munch, J.; Cabello, E. M.; Bonny, O.; Wagner, C. A.; Bachmann-Gagescu, R.
after.abstract: Background: The majority of rare diseases are caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene with Mendelian inheritance. In contrast, common diseases typically have complex genetic etiology, ranging from a cumulative impact of many common genetic variants with small individual effects, to fewer rare variants with larger effects, with monogenic forms at the rare end of the spectrum. While unknown prevalence of the monogenic fraction of common diseases and incomplete penetrance make identification of such monogenic forms of common diseases particularly challenging, their diagnosis can be essential for precision medicine. Automated rare variant prioritization tools, such as Exomiser, aid whole exome sequencing-based rare genetic disease diagnostics. However, Exomiser's utility has not been systematically assessed in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases prior to this study. Methods: We evaluated and optimized Exomiser for prioritization of rare pathogenic variants in common disease using a large kidney stone disease (KSD) cohort (701 cases, 200 controls). First, we benchmarked Exomiser's performance across different settings for KSD "gold standard" variants in established KSD genes with Mendelian inheritance. Next, we utilized the optimal pipeline for discovery of novel KSD genes and compared Exomiser's findings with results from gene-level rare variant enrichment analyses in an extended in-house cohort and the UK Biobank. Results: With the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all (94%, N = 48) previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated 62 novel genes predominantly involved in ion homeostasis, which are now available to the scientific community as candidate genes for KSD. Out of these genes, orthogonal approaches also support ABCC6 as a strong KSD risk gene, in line with previous research, providing a proof-of-principle supporting the utility of Exomiser in the context of common disease. Conclusions: This study serves as an example for automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases, which is a key step for precision medicine.

after.title: Preprint: Additional Vascular Imaging in Women With Acute Cerebral Ischemia: Thresholds for Cost-Effectiveness
after.authors: Boettger, P.; Klug, J.; Agarwal, A.; Alhaj Omar, O.; Juenemann, M.; Buerke, M.; Sossalla, S.; Carrera, E.
after.abstract: Background: Women with acute cerebral ischemia receive intracranial vascular imaging less often than men, but the value of expanding imaging is uncertain. We estimated the treatment rates and functional benefits required for additional imaging to be cost-effective. Methods: We developed a decision tree and state-transition model comparing additional imaging followed by timely endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for M1 occlusion with current care from Ontario public-payer and US Medicare perspectives. Women-specific 90-day modified Rankin Scale distributions from HERMES were projected over a lifetime. We jointly varied the proportion of additional scans leading to additional timely EVT and the treatment effect relative to HERMES. Cost-effectiveness thresholds were CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. Program costs represented health-care resources in Ontario and additional payments under Medicare. Results: At variable program costs of CAD 1,000 or USD 1,000 per additional scan, assuming the full HERMES effect and no additional fixed costs or pathway-related harm, expected cost-effectiveness required one additional timely EVT per 48 scans in Ontario and 57 under Medicare (2.07% and 1.74%, respectively). Treatment rates of 3.07% and 2.65% were required for a 90% probability of cost-effectiveness under these assumptions. At three additional thrombectomies per 100 scans and the same costs, treatment effects had to reach 76.9% and 67.3% of the HERMES effect. With the full effect, 1,000 additional scans at this treatment rate yielded approximately 5 additional functionally independent survivors at 90 days. Deterministic analyses restricted to 5 years increased the required treatment rates to 4.44% and 4.22%. Conclusions: Additional vascular imaging in women could be cost-effective when a small proportion of scans leads to timely thrombectomy, provided sufficient functional benefit is retained. Prospective evaluations should assess additional treatment opportunities, functional outcomes and program costs against these conditional thresholds, which depend on projected long-term outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Asking Conversational Artificial Intelligence about Health and Subsequent Actions among Adults in Japan: A Cross-sectional Web Survey
after.authors: Ichikawa, M.
after.abstract: Introduction: People increasingly ask conversational artificial intelligence (AI) about health; however, how this relates to care seeking in Japan, where universal health coverage renders care accessible, remains unknown. This study described how many adults ask AI about health, why and when, what they do afterward, and how much they trust AI compared with other sources. Methods: This two-stage cross-sectional survey employed a commercial web panel (October-November 2026). A screening survey of adults aged [≥]20 years (10,000 responses; 8,209 analyzed) estimated prevalence. A main survey of users (1,000 responses; 735 analyzed) asked about purposes, the most recent use and subsequent actions, and trust in seven information sources. Responses were weighted by sex and age. Results: In the past 6 months, 40.3% of adults (95% confidence interval, 39.3-41.4) asked conversational AI about health. The most recent use occurred before a medical visit for 39.0%, after a visit for 23.4%, and when no visit was being considered for 37.6%. Subsequently, 35.4% visited a medical facility; 12.8% (10.3-15.3) decided not to visit or postponed a visit (5.1% of all adults). Forgoing or delaying was more frequent among users with high trust in AI (trusting it completely or a lot; 22.5% vs. 10.9% among others). Among pre-visit users, it was less frequent with high trust in health professionals (16.7% vs. 30.9%) and did not clearly differ by trust in AI. Of users, 61.4% had high trust in health professionals and 14.3% in AI. Conclusions: In Japan, approximately 4 in 10 adults asked AI about health, and 1 in 8 users forwent or delayed a visit. This was more common with high trust in AI; among pre-visit users, it was associated with low trust in health professionals. How trust in AI and health professionals relates to care seeking warrants further study.

Objective: To develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. Methods: RoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. Results: In ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% ({kappa} 0.35) and 53.5% ({kappa} 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% ({kappa} 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% ({kappa} 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% ({kappa} 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% ({kappa} 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% ({kappa} 0.16), 47.3% ({kappa} 0.17), 31.0% ({kappa} 0.03) and 46.5% ({kappa} 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%. On the 52 ROBoto2 trials rated by two assessors, the second assessor's sensitivity for the reference assessor's high-risk domains was 23.1% (specificity 90.3%) and RoB-BERT's was 30.8% (specificity 92.7%). RoB-BERT located 95.7% of its quotations verbatim in the report and cost US$0.005 per trial, 2% to 6% of the frontier models' cost. Conclusions: RoB-BERT agreed with single human assessors at least as closely as two human assessors agreed with each other, and matched or exceeded frontier LLMs at a fraction of their cost. The results show the poor reliability of human assessors using RoB 2 and the need for consensus ratings, with RoB-BERT potentially serving as one rater.

after.authors: Kallis, K.; Kumar, P.; Kang-Sim, E.; Neels, N.; Deng, J.; Quitevis, C. R.; Alsaigh, T.; Ross, E. G.
after.abstract: Background: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is associated with substantial cardiovascular and limb-related morbidity, making long-term cardiovascular prevention an important part of care. However, longitudinal patterns of guideline-based quality measure achievement after PAD diagnosis remain poorly characterized in broad clinical populations. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Epic Cosmos electronic health record (EHR) data to identify adults aged 18 to 75 years with PAD diagnosed from 2019 to 2023. Four cardiovascular prevention components based on Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Quality Measures were assessed annually after PAD diagnosis: blood pressure target achievement, documented tobacco-free status, antiplatelet therapy, and statin therapy. Complete achievement was defined as meeting all four measures. We assessed quality-measure achievement across groups, three-year quality-index trends, and associations between complete achievement and subsequent outcomes. Results: Among 906,686 patients, model-adjusted first-year achievement was 60.6% for tobacco-free status, 61.9% for blood pressure control, 39.5% for antiplatelet therapy, and 63.4% for statin therapy; 10.4% achieved all four. Model-adjusted complete achievement was 12.4% in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), 10.5% in claudication, and 10.2% in unspecified PAD. Model-adjusted rates varied by sex, race/ethnicity, insurance type, rurality, PAD severity, and comorbidities and ranged from 7.6% to 14.7%. Complete achievement in year 1 was associated with lower adjusted odds of amputation (odds ratio (OR), 0.91), vascular procedures (OR, 0.86), stroke (OR, 0.90), and myocardial infarction (OR, 0.94). Conclusions: In this large national EHR cohort, individual quality measures improved after PAD diagnosis, but only 10.4% of patients achieved all four assessed components during the first year after diagnosis. Differences across quality domains and patient subgroups highlight variation in longitudinal cardiovascular risk prevention, particularly among patients with less clinically apparent disease.

after.title: Preprint: Evaluation of a Brief Educational Intervention to Improve Healthcare Provider Communication About Autism Genetic Testing
after.authors: Pilson, O. G.; Barna, L. S.; Grimes, T.; Salako, T. A.; Ramirez-Renta, G. M.; Wang, A.; Gunter, C.
after.abstract: Although professional guidelines recommend offering genetic testing following an autism diagnosis, uptake remains low in the United States. Healthcare providers frequently report limited education and uncertainty discussing autism genetics with patients and families. We developed and evaluated a brief educational intervention to improve provider communication about autism genetic testing, consisting of animated videos addressing autism genetics, available testing options, and strategies for discussing testing with autistic individuals and families. We evaluated the intervention among 100 U.S.-based healthcare providers and a community panel of 99 autistic adults. Participants completed a validated measure of genetic literacy before viewing the videos, then evaluated the intervention and its perceived impact on genetic testing. Providers showed higher genetic literacy than the general U.S. population, yet only 23% reported frequently discussing genetic testing before the intervention. Afterward, 86% reported greater likelihood of recommending genetic testing following diagnosis, and 88% reported the videos changed how they would discuss genetics with patients and families. Both cohorts rated the resources favorably, and 71% of autistic adults reported greater likelihood of pursuing genetic testing after viewing the videos. Brief, communication-focused educational resources may improve workflows for autism genetic testing and support informed decision-making for providers, autistic individuals, and their families.

after.authors: Dragostinov, Y.; Hsu, R. E.; Ennis, G. W.; Londono-Correa, D.; Schwaba, T.; Nivard, M. G.; Tucker-Drob, E. M.
after.abstract: Polygenic indices (PGIs) are downwardly biased in their predictive accuracies in independent samples due to the presence of estimation error in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) from which they are constructed. By performing GWAS of the same phenotype in independent samples, we obtain to error-corrected estimates of PGI prediction accuracy, which we use to estimate the extent to which different PGI construction methods (unadjusted, Clumping, LDpred2-inf, LDpred2-auto, SBayesR, PRS-CS-auto) index total single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) heritability. To ensure practicality of this approach when individual-level data from the original GWAS are not available, we provide a means of synthetically splitting existing GWAS summary statistics into independent halves. In both simulated and empirical data, we find that advanced PGI construction methods that produce enhanced uncorrected prediction accuracies (often by shrinking individual SNP effects towards zero or exactly to zero) also produce deflated error-corrected prediction accuracies. LDpred2-inf, which most closely resembles a multiple regression estimator to account for linkage disequilibrium without further aggressive shrinkage, consistently produces PGIs with relatively lower uncorrected prediction accuracies but higher error-corrected prediction accuracies that nearly fully recover SNP heritability. We show that PGI construction methods that implement aggressive shrinkage may also provide biased patterns of associations with collateral phenotypes, irrespective of error correction. By providing a means of straightforwardly obtaining error-corrected estimates of prediction accuracy using PGIs derived from standard GWAS summary statistics, we have highlighted an uncommonly recognized bias-variance tradeoff associated with the choice of PGI construction methods.

after.authors: Perez-Elena, M. A.; Salvoro, C.; Matias, D.; Satari, L.; Puiggros, M.; Zugasti, D.; Alonso-Parrilla, L.; Torrents, D.
after.abstract: X chromosome (Xchr) contribution to complex traits remains incomplete, due to its unique inheritance pattern and its inactivation mechanism. Therefore, we gathered data from 800,000 individuals from the UK Biobank and dbGaP, and performed a sex-stratified phenome-wide association study of Xchr variation across 3,741 complex traits. Heritability analyses revealed sex-specific patterns and an overall involvement of Xchr in complex phenotypes. We identified 6,531 loci significantly associated with 402 complex traits, with a higher proportion of associations consistent with dominant inheritance than observed for autosomes. Although effect directions were largely concordant between sexes, loci with significant effect-size differences were enriched for escape-gene associations. Escape genes were depleted among trait-associated loci and strongly enriched for risky disease effects. These association patterns enabled prediction of escape status for unannotated genes. This overview of Xchr contribution to complex traits suggests inactivation escape as a clear risky feature for females.
